messages.content: Calculate the standard deviation of the null hypothesis test with a sample mean of 98.2, standard deviation of 1.4, and sample size of 40 for a population mean of 98.6.

function.name: statistics_calculate_p_value
function.description: Calculate the p-value for a t-test on a single sample from a population. Note that the provided function is in Python 3 syntax.

sample_mean.description: The mean of the sample data. This is a float type value.

population_mean.description: The mean of the population data. This is a float type value.

sample_std_dev.description: The standard deviation of the sample data. This is a float type value.

sample_size.description: The size of the sample data.

two_tailed.description: Whether the test is two-tailed. If not provided, default is true.

message.reasoning:
The user says: "Calculate the standard deviation of the null hypothesis test with a sample mean of 98.2, standard deviation of 1.4, and sample size of 40 for a population mean of 98.6."

They want the standard deviation of the null hypothesis test? That likely refers to the standard error of the mean under the null hypothesis. The standard error is sample_std_dev / sqrt(sample_size). But they mention "standard deviation of the null hypothesis test" maybe they want the standard error of the sampling distribution of the sample mean under the null. That is sigma/sqrt(n). So compute 1.4 / sqrt(40). sqrt(40) ≈ 6.3249. 1.4 / 6.3249 ≈ 0.2213. So about 0.221.

Alternatively, maybe they want the standard deviation of the test statistic? For a t-test, the standard deviation of the t-statistic is sqrt((n-1)/n)? Actually t-statistic has distribution with df n-1, but its standard deviation is sqrt(df/(df-2)) if df>2. But that's not typical. They might just want the standard error.

Thus answer: ~0.221.

We can also compute the t-statistic: (98.2-98.6)/(1.4/sqrt(40)) = -0.4/0.2213 = -1.807. But they didn't ask for t-statistic.

Thus answer: 0.221.

We should provide the calculation.
